Some free agents: George Springer, Trent Grisham, Ian Happ, Seiya Suzuki (Q), Randy Arozarena, Taylor Ward, Daulton Varsho, Adolis Garcia, Luis Robert Jr., Randal Grichuk, Myles Straw, Lane Thomas

Designated hitter
Some free agents: Joc Pederson, Dominic Smith

Starting pitcher
Dustin May signs with White Sox
May, 29, made 31 mostly league-average starts for the Cardinals and eventual champion Brewers this season -- many of them quite abbreviated. In fact, he ended up averaging fewer than four innings over his 10 Brewers starts and he did not qualify for the ERA title. The desperate White Sox figure to allow May to go deeper into games, but that comes at a cost, since he posted a 4.70 ERA and a 1.32 WHIP with only 0.4 bWAR last season.

Hey, at least May stayed healthy, which is a feat for him. Plus, he was a bit unlucky, as his 3.54 FIP indicates. However, that doesn't mean May warrants inclusion in ESPN standard drafts, with a preliminary points-league rank outside the top 75 starting pitchers. -- Karabell (11/17)

Other free agents: Tarik Skubal, Michael King, Sonny Gray, Robbie Ray, Brandon Woodruff, Zac Gallen, Shota Imanaga, Kevin Gausman, Chris Bassitt, Jack Flaherty, Jameson Taillon, Max Scherzer, Clay Holmes, Matthew Boyd, Nick Pivetta, Shane Bieber, Freddy Peralta, Trevor Rogers (Q), Nick Martinez, Tyler Mahle, Foster Griffin, Michael Soroka

Relief pitcher
RHP Emilio Pagan signs with Tigers
Pagan, 35, saved 57 games for the Cincinnati Reds over the past two seasons, although his 2025 numbers were rather ordinary (3.38 ERA, 25.9% K rate). Still, this is a franchise that desired Kenley Jansen and let him save 22 games last season even though there were better pitchers in the bullpen. Pagan produced nearly identical stats to Jansen. In other words, Pagan isn't so valuable -- but if all you care about are saves in a roto format, a healthy Pagan should provide at least 25 of them. -- Karabell (11/13)

RHP Evan Phillips signs with Braves
Phillips, 32, posted a 2.36 ERA over parts of six seasons for the Los Angeles Dodgers. He also accrued 42 combined saves during 2023 and 2024. He missed most of 2025 dealing with Tommy John surgery and returned last season to pitch 26 effective innings. Additionally, Phillips has never permitted a run over 18⅓ postseason innings. The Braves figure to turn to RHP Robert Suarez to close (because Raisel Iglesias is a free agent), but a healthy Phillips should accrue ample holds as well as occasional saves. -- Karabell (11/13)

stories.body:
Manchester City are in talks with Matheus Nunes about extending his contract at the Etihad Stadium, sources have told ESPN.

Nunes has a deal until 2028, but City are keen to agree fresh terms. Negotiations are ongoing, although sources have told ESPN that talks are not yet at an advanced stage.

The Portugal international is closing in on 150 appearances for the club after arriving from Wolves in 2023. Initially joining as a midfielder, he was converted to a full-back under former boss Pep Guardiola.

Nunes appeared in 34 of City's 38 Premier League games last season with his form convincing club bosses to strengthen other areas of the squad over the summer instead of at right-back.

Meanwhile, City are facing a decision about whether to keep midfielder Mateo Kovacic. The Croatian is out of contract at the end of the season and can negotiate with clubs outside the Premier League from January.

Kovacic has struggled for game time so far this season and has made just one Premier League start under new manager Enzo Maresca.

stories.headline: Harrison returns to lead overhaul of women's divisional rankings
stories.summary: Here's a look at every weight class to determine the best of the best in UFC, PFL and beyond.
stories.body:
All three women's MMA weight classes in the ESPN divisional rankings have new No. 1 fighters. One of them also has a new No. 2.

The division with the most dramatic changes is women's bantamweight, where Kayla Harrison reclaimed the top spot in her return to the rankings after being ineligible because of more than a year of inactivity. She successfully defended her championship at UFC 334 with a fourth-round submission of another returnee, Amanda Nunes, who had been retired for nearly 3½ years. Nunes is back in the 135-pound rankings as well, at No. 2.

The women's bantamweight top 10 also welcomes Bia Mesquita, who made quick work of then-ranked Macy Chiasson on Saturday at UFC 334. Mesquita makes her rankings debut at No. 9, and Chiasson is out.

Women's flyweight and strawweight acquired their new top-ranked fighters not via returns from inactivity but by inactivity itself. Neither flyweight Valentina Shevchenko nor strawweight Zhang Weili has competed in over a year, so both former champions are newly ineligible. The rest of the fighters in those two top 10s all move up a spot, with the UFC champions in each division, flyweight Natalia Silva and strawweight Mackenzie Dern, taking over as the new No. 1s. Tracy Cortez enters the flyweight rankings at No. 10, and at strawweight, Denise Gomes is newly ranked fifth and Yan Xiaonan is 10th.

The only men's division with changes to the rankings is heavyweight -- but the change does not affect the No. 1 position, where Ciryl Gane remains after successfully defending his title at UFC 334. The man he beat, Josh Hokit, moves up three spots to No. 4 after a resilient showing against Gane. Dropping from the rankings: Vadim Nemkov, who lost for the first time in a decade at the PFL's event in Dubai on Saturday. He dropped the PFL title to Sergei Bilostenniy.

Here are the ESPN pound-for-pound MMA rankings and a list of current UFC champions in all weight classes.

Results are current; rankings as of Nov. 17. To be eligible for the rankings, a fighter must have competed over the past 12 months or must have an upcoming fight booked. Fighters who have been dropped for inactivity can be reinstated only after they compete.

stories.headline: MLS Cup playoff Power Rankings: Can history-making Nashville be stopped?
stories.summary: Nashville just won the Supporters' Shield with a league-record points haul, so naturally it tops ESPN's MLS Cup playoff Power Rankings.
stories.body:
It's Monday, and while MLS wasn't in action over the weekend in observance of the international break, the playoffs begin Thursday, which means it's the perfect time for ESPN's MLS Cup playoff Power Rankings.

Who's primed for a deep postseason run culminating in winning MLS Cup on Dec. 18? Which club with title aspirations is in jeopardy of an early exit? Joseph Lowery ranks all 18 playoff sides from first to worst.

1. Nashville SC
Final regular-season ranking: 1st

Conference seed: 1st in East

Next match: vs. Orlando City (8) or FC Cincinnati (9), Nov. 22, 8:30 p.m. ET

Not only did Nashville claim the Supporters' Shield as the best team in the regular season, but it also set MLS' single-season points record with 77 along the way. With a truly elite shot stopper in Brian Schwake, a back line with multiple Defender of the Year candidates, a flexible midfield and a star-studded attack, the Music City side has the tools to go all the way.

2. Vancouver Whitecaps
Final regular-season ranking: 6th

Conference seed: 1st in West

Next match: vs. Seattle Sounders (8) or Real Salt Lake (9), Nov. 22, 4 p.m. ET

There's a case to be made for the Whitecaps to top this list, given they led the league in expected goal (xG) differential this season. While Sebastian Berhalter's summer exit and Thomas Müller's recent fitness issues knock them out of contention for top spot in the rankings, don't be surprised if Vancouver makes it one step further than last year and lifts the championship trophy.

3. Inter Miami CF
Final regular-season ranking: 2nd

Conference seed: 2nd in East

Next match: vs. Columbus Crew (7), Nov. 21, 6 p.m. ET

It wasn't always pretty for Miami in 2026, with three different managers on the sideline over the course of the year, but moving on from Sergio Busquets and Jordi Alba was never going to be easy. Still, with Lionel Messi patrolling the attack and the most talented team in the league behind him, Inter Miami reminded viewers that they can hit heights no other MLS outfit can -- even if they have a lower floor than some of the other primary contenders.

4. Philadelphia Union
Final regular-season ranking: 7th

Conference seed: 6th in East

Next match: at New England Revolution (3), Nov. 21, 2 p.m. ET

If you'd merely glanced at this year's playoff bracket prior to reading this piece, perhaps you bristled at the sixth seed in the East landing this high. But after a league-worst run before the FIFA World Cup break, only Nashville posted more points than Philadelphia after the summer. Interim head coach Ryan Richter has his team humming heading into the postseason.

5. St. Louis City SC
Final regular-season ranking: 4th

Conference seed: 3rd in West

Next match: vs. LAFC (6), Nov. 23, 8 p.m. ET

Undoubtedly, St. Louis' rebuild is well ahead of schedule. After an offseason filled with front office and coaching changes, STL spent this season lifting the U.S. Open Cup trophy and setting a league record for consecutive games without a loss. Although a busy season seems to be taking its toll, City have both the talent and the tactical principles to make a deep run.

6. Chicago Fire
Final regular-season ranking: 5th

Conference seed: 4th in East

Next match: vs. Charlotte FC (5), Nov. 22, 6:30 p.m. ET

Robert Lewandowski's arrival in Chicago was supposed to supercharge the Fire. While that hasn't happened (their xG per game dropped from 2.15 before the former Bayern Munich and Barcelona star's arrival to 1.86 afterward), Gregg Berhalter's team is still among the deepest in this year's postseason field. No one should be surprised if the Fire's attack clicks this winter and propels them to a trophy.

7. New England Revolution
Final regular-season ranking: 3rd

Conference seed: 3rd in East

Next match: vs. Philadelphia Union (6), Nov. 21, 2 p.m. ET

Armed with Matt Turner in goal, who recently concluded the most dominant shot-stopping regular season in MLS history, according to American Soccer Analysis' goals prevented metric, the Revs won't be an easy team to beat. Really, though, they need a healthy combination of Jack Harrison and Peyton Miller to support Carles Gil in the attack if they are to enjoy a lengthy stay in the postseason.

8. San Jose Earthquakes
Final regular-season ranking: 12th

Conference seed: 4th in West

Next match: vs. Houston Dynamo (5), Nov. 24, 10 p.m. ET

Back at the beginning of the season, Niko Tsakiris and Timo Werner had the Earthquakes looking like world-beaters. Then, both of those dynamic attackers fell injured, and they have struggled to regain their full fitness ever since. They've started together just one time since August. That one time, however, came on Decision Day. If Tsakiris and Werner can stay on the field together in the playoffs, San Jose will have an outside chance.

9. FC Dallas
Final regular-season ranking: 8th

Conference seed: 2nd in West

Next match: vs. Portland Timbers (7), Nov. 21, 4 p.m. ET

Quite a lot changed for Dallas toward the end of the regular season: Daniel Job arrived in the summer transfer window to provide nearly unparalleled speed in the front line alongside Petar Musa, while manager Eric Quill appeared to rewrite some of his side's tactical programming. The result? A team that's more dangerous with the ball than ever before in 2026 but one that's even harder to predict.

10. Charlotte FC
Final regular-season ranking: 10th

Conference seed: 5th in East

Next match: at Chicago Fire (4), Nov. 22, 6:30 p.m. ET

One of MLS' models of consistency, Charlotte put together yet another solid season. While Dean Smith's team is far more dangerous in the attack this year than in the past with Pep Biel, Allan Saint-Maximin and some impressive young wingers leading the charge, it is also more vulnerable defensively. It's hard to picture this imbalanced Charlotte team sustaining a postseason run.

11. Columbus Crew
Final regular-season ranking: 18th

Conference seed: 7th in East

Next match: at Inter Miami (2), Nov. 21, 6 p.m. ET

After a brutal start to 2026 that featured a season-ending injury to striker Wessam Abou Ali and a coaching change, the Crew were incredibly busy during the summer window. Between their vigorous transfer business and the time spent under interim manager Laurent Courtois' tutelage, wins started coming for Columbus. Inconsistency still rules at times for the Crew, but they're certainly hot heading into the playoffs.

12. LAFC
Final regular-season ranking: 9th

Conference seed: 6th in West

Next match: at St. Louis City (3), Nov. 23, 8 p.m. ET

It's almost unthinkable that a team with Son Heung-Min, Denis Bouanga and tons of other quality players could be so bleak, but it's been that sort of year for LAFC. Those two superstars haven't linked up in the same way they did to close out last season. Marc Dos Santos failed to maximize them and paid for it with his job. Interim coach Xavi Tamarit hasn't cracked the code, either. Instead of a terrifying, forward-thinking outfit, LAFC have been scratching and clawing for results all season.

13. Portland Timbers
Final regular-season ranking: 19th

Conference seed: 7th in West

Next match: at FC Dallas (2), Nov. 21, 4 p.m. ET

It wasn't long ago that all signs pointed toward Portland missing out on the postseason. Instead, new manager Martí Cifuentes, who took over for Phil Neville midseason, has the Timbers playing an impressively cohesive style. Since the Spaniard's first game in charge, Portland ranks 10th in MLS in xG differential per game, according to American Soccer Analysis. Kristoffer Velde doesn't have enough help in the attack for this team to be a true threat, but progress is being made.

14. Houston Dynamo
Final regular-season ranking: 16th

Conference seed: 5th in West

Next match: at San Jose Earthquakes (4), Nov. 24, 10 p.m. ET

Although it finished fifth in the West, no playoff team scored fewer goals in the regular season than Houston. It's those attacking limitations that will hold the Dynamo back in the playoffs. Outside of Brazilian newcomer Guilherme, they lack the sort of repeatable chance creation that fuels a run to MLS Cup.

15. Seattle Sounders
Final regular-season ranking: 13th

Conference seed: 8th in West

Next match: vs. Real Salt Lake (9), Nov. 19, 10 p.m. ET

Fully healthy and able to lean on their mixture of talent and experience, the Sounders would be a threat to win MLS Cup, but manager Brian Schmetzer simply doesn't have a complete squad at his disposal -- nor has he for most of the year. Jordan Morris' first-half exit on Decision Day was just the latest in a long line of fitness issues that have turned Seattle's season upside down.

16. Real Salt Lake
Final regular-season ranking: 21st

Conference seed: 8th in East

Next match: at Seattle Sounders (8), Nov. 19, 10 p.m. ET

With Zavier Gozo and Diego Luna still in the lineup, lifting a trophy would have been possible for Salt Lake. With Gozo now playing for Crystal Palace after a summer move and Luna out for the year with an injury, RSL are simply too short on weapons. There are quality players in Utah, but a postseason path that begins with a road game in Seattle before a potential Vancouver series will be too much to handle.

17. Orlando City
Final regular-season ranking: 11th

Conference seed: 8th in East

Next match: vs. FC Cincinnati (9), Nov. 19, 7:30 p.m. ET

As brilliant as Antoine Griezmann is, even the best player in MLS not named Lionel Messi can't paper over all the cracks in Orlando's defensive setup. Orlando City conceded 78 goals in the regular season, good for the second most in one campaign in league history. There's an entire season's worth of evidence that points to Orlando's inability to control leads, win games and lift a trophy.

18. FC Cincinnati
Final regular-season ranking: 15th

Conference seed: 9th in East

Next match: at Orlando City (8), Nov. 19, 7:30 p.m. ET

So many of Orlando City's issues also apply to Cincinnati: Pat Noonan's team conceded a staggering 75 goals and had to be rescued by brilliant attacking play in the regular season. Like Orlando, Cincinnati lacks the defensive consistency to win a wild-card game and handle business on the road this winter.

stories.headline: Key defender Mitch Harris bolting up AFL Draft boards at the eleventh hour
stories.summary: There are risers and sliders every year, but the bolting Mitch Harris has recruiters in raptures like few others this AFL Draft cycle.
stories.body:
There are risers and sliders every year, but the bolting Mitch Harris has recruiters in raptures like few others this AFL Draft cycle.

The South Australian is the ideal key defensive prospect; at 196cm he averaged 5.2 intercept marks per game at SANFL U18s level, headlined by a game with 12 intercept marks across the backline. He went and backed it up at League level through a finals campaign for Woodville-West Torrens averaging 1.8 intercept marks, and was the best-performing key defender at the national championships.'

Intercepting is only half his game -- Harris is a defender first and foremost. He takes on the biggest forward each week and displays the timing, anticipation, physicality and competitiveness that befits the game's best key backs.

They're the hallmark traits that will see him taken with a top 10 pick at the AFL Draft.

"It's something I want to improve on, the offensive side," Harris admitted to ESPN. "But the defensive acts as my role as a key defender, your job is to stop the key forwards and stop them kicking goals and I guess from that you try to get some offensive ball.

"Defend first sort of mentality, that's my job and that's what I've got to do.

"You look back on it now, and I'm not a high disposal-getting player, I would've averaged 10 touches during League or similar to that at the champs, but still having an impact without the ball. Aerially impacting or just stopping you forward from getting it, a lot of the time it doesn't really come up on the stat sheet but it still has an impact on the game."

Harris's star rose to the precipice of the top bracket of prospects after a five-game stint at SANFL League level to finish the year. With WWT he featured in three finals and wasn't overawed by the occasion as an 18-year-old against seasoned professionals.

"I'm pretty happy with it. Just the ability to play consistent footy and then the opportunities in the SANFL League. I'm pretty grateful for that.

"The bigger bodies and the speed of the game, it was so quick and quick transition and I guess the skills even. A lot of the kicks were impossible to stop, if that makes sense.

"Those three finals were the best footy I've been a part of and the most enjoyable. It was just surreal."

Harris was a standout in nailbiting one-goal wins through to a preliminary final with desperate defensive actions on talls and smalls.

His size and athletic foundation allows him to play through the air but also close space at ground level and find the angles to chop off fast transition.

It's an element of his game clubs were keen to see more of and it came to fruition on the biggest stage.

"My hardest matchup [in junior footy] was probably Sam Gayfer for Vic Metro. Credit to him, he's pretty smart and uses his body well. Vic Metro, the way they moved the ball up and down the ground and his smarts to get on the lead was pretty hard to stop at times.

"I like just taking their key forward and doing that job. Having reference of your opponent, like if you know they want to wrestle then don't get in a wrestle. Use your strengths of being athletic to impact.

"Even throughout the League stuff I'd find myself as a tall on smaller players. I was always so used to playing on the tallest forward so it was something different and I think in the long run it's probably helped me a little bit as well. It sort of shows you can play on both sides and if not it was just a good learning experience in how they go about it as well."

It wasn't all smooth sailing for Harris in 2026. He fought through an early-season concussion and then dealt with pneumonia in a crucial stage of the year before an ankle injury the week prior to the AFL Draft combine ruled him out of testing.

Despite all that, it was his most injury-free campaign through the elite junior pathways that gave him a timely platform to rise up draft boards.

"I don't think I was going to do the 2km, because I've had pneumonia. It was a pretty hectic couple of weeks, and after the Sturt game I was getting worse and I thought it was just the same pneumonia and it turns out I had rhinovirus, conveniently.

"I finally got into things last week and then hurt my ankle playing basketball.

"It was the first year I'd had a clean run, I blamed it on my growth a bit but it was my first proper pre-season and everything." Harris's mental preparation through injury layoffs and leading into games has been an important step forward in his footy journey.

Often restless and dealing with performance anxiety, his preparation throughout the week has seen his game elevate to the next level.

"I used to get really nervous, where I couldn't sleep much. Now I'm not too bad, I get a good night's sleep and even in the morning. It's only sort of when I get there prior to the game I get pretty nervous.

"As soon as the game starts it sort of all goes away and I'm fine but the arrival is when I start to get butterflies.

"For me, if I'm organised and doing things right throughout the week I know I'm going to sort of play well, if that makes sense. I try and be really organised and if I'm training well and doing all the little things throughout the week I'm confident that I'll play well on the weekends. That's helped heaps as well."

The South Australian prospect is now entrenched in the top 10 on draft night. His range starts with Richmond at pick five and Melbourne has been one of his biggest admirers at the following selection, trading up the board with the key defender in their mix.

His draft range may only extend to the Swans at pick seven, with the premiership contenders excited by the chance to draft a readymade defender with their first pick since stalwart Dane Rampe's off-season retirement.

It puts Harris out of the reckoning of local teams Port Adelaide and Adelaide, and will mean moving away from his parents for the first time.

"I have a bit of white line fever, like as soon as you cross the line I hate to get beaten. I think it's a family trait, we're all super competitive, determined to not get beat and be super ruthless.

"Mum and Dad, they only want the best for all of us, my older brother and younger sister.. In a perfect world you stay in SA but I would be happy going anywhere given the opportunity."

stories.headline: As Nike replaces Adidas, is UEFA Champions League star ball on its way out?
stories.summary: Nike will replace Adidas as supplier of UEFA Champions League match balls from next season. Will the famous 'star ball' design soon be no more?
stories.body:
Editor's note: This article was first published on Aug. 26, 2026 and has been updated

The UEFA Champions League and UEFA Women's Champions League match balls will boast a brand new look starting next season after UEFA confirmed on Monday that Nike will be taking over from long-standing provider Adidas as the official supplier for the 2027-28 campaign onwards.

Nike will take the reins for the 2027-28 campaign onward after agreeing a deal to supply the official match balls for all three UEFA club competitions from 2027 to 2031 -- the Champions League, the Europa League and the Conference League. According to The Guardian, that deal is worth around $45 million a year, double the value of the final contract with Adidas.

- Man United, Pochettino's to-do list based on what's gone wrong

- Meet Como's Paz, the heir to Messi's Argentina No. 10 shirt

- Champions League talking points: Are Como the real deal?

With Adidas having supplied the official Champions League match ball since 2001, the "star ball" design has become an emblem of the competition. However, the last we see of the iconic pattern might be in the 2026-27 final.

That's because, as things stand, there are no specific details available as to the designs that Nike has in store. In a statement on Monday, UEFA would only say: "Further details on the match ball designs will be revealed in due course." It is also unclear -- and highly unlikely -- that the American sportswear giant will continue with the star theme popularised by Adidas over the past 25 years, as the German powerhouse reportedly hold the rights to the star ball design.

Nike's designs are therefore likely to be fresh and distinct with the intent of drawing a line under Adidas' tenure as UEFA match ball suppliers while also launching their own, modernised visual identity.

Back in August, Adidas unveiled what will be their final iteration of the "star ball," the preliminary eye-catching colourway of which is currently being used throughout the group phase of the 2026-27 Champions League.

The men's version of the 2026-27 Champions League ball is plastered in a neon-spattered livery that, according to Adidas, has been inspired by players creating colourful moments of magic and personal expression while plugging away at training on cold, foggy training pitches during their quest to attain Champions League greatness.

The design for the women's match ball is a little less abstract. The golden-orange pattern takes its inspiration from the aura of the ring of 11 stars that make up the UWCL emblem, with flashes of metallic purple and silver then adding a dash of visual contrast to the mix.

Both balls are based on the template that Adidas have used for their Champions League match balls since the introduction of the "Finale 1" ball for the 2001-02 season. Since then, over 50 iterations of the UCL star ball have been deployed in the competition -- and that's not including the various hi-vis yellow variants that have been used in winter months over the years.

stories.headline: 2027 WNBA mock draft: Tempo win lottery, projected to pick JuJu Watkins at No. 1
stories.summary: Toronto edged Houston and got the top pick in Sunday's draft lottery. The Comets will pick No. 2 and the Mystics No. 3.
stories.body:
In what could be the JuJu Watkins sweepstakes, the Toronto Tempo will have the No. 1 pick in the 2027 WNBA draft. The Tempo won the draft lottery Sunday, with the Houston Comets picking second and the Washington Mystics third.

The Seattle Storm have the No. 4 pick, the Portland Fire got No. 5 and the Los Angeles Sparks have Nos. 6 and 7.

The Tempo, an expansion team in 2026, finished 11-33 last season, missing the playoffs. They were last in the league in defensive rating and won just one game after the All-Star break.

All of that could be much improved in 2027 with a player such as Watkins in Toronto. The national player of the year as a sophomore for the USC Trojans, Watkins missed last season after a knee injury suffered in the 2025 NCAA tournament. She has looked great so far this season and would fit in well with any WNBA team.

This is just Watkins' third college season, but age-wise, she is eligible for the draft. It is unknown if she will go pro or return to USC, but for now we are including her in the mock draft. If she decides Toronto is an unappealing destination or just wants to spend another season in college, she can wait until the 2028 draft.

That said, there is also uncertainty about the seniors who already have completed three seasons. Under the NCAA's new age-based eligibility model -- the five-seasons-in-five-years rule -- they could return for the 2027-28 season. So a lot about the draft pool remains speculative.

But now we know the lottery order.

1. Toronto Tempo: JuJu Watkins
USC | guard | 6-foot-2 | senior

Watkins and the Trojans are 3-1 after a close loss Sunday to No. 1 South Carolina in which she had 25 points. The March 2025 knee injury that forced Watkins to miss last season has not slowed her. She is averaging 24.5 points, 6.8 rebounds, 3.5 assists and 3.3 steals. The Tempo's strength last season was at guard, led by Marina Mabrey. If Watkins doesn't declare for the draft, there should still be good players available for the Tempo. But perhaps not an immediate franchise-changer as Watkins is expected to be.

2. Houston Comets: Madison Booker
Texas | forward | 6-foot-1 | senior

Like several teams, Texas has not been tested yet. But Booker has displayed why she's a lottery pick in the three games she has played so far, including a 30-point, six-assist game against Northern Colorado. Booker's size, strength and confidence on offense and her versatility on defense should translate to the pro game. She took a hard fall in Wednesday's win over South Dakota State and did not play in Sunday's victory against Tarleton State, but she is not expected to miss much more time. The Comets -- the Connecticut Sun relocated as a revived franchise -- last played in the 2008 WNBA season. The Sun were tied for next to last with Toronto at 11-33 this year, and it's fair to say they could use help in all areas, which would make Booker appealing.

3. Washington Mystics: Hannah Hidalgo
Notre Dame | guard | 5-foot-6 | senior

Hidalgo has carried a heavy load throughout her college career, and that continues her senior season. In four victories, she has averaged 28.3 points, 7.5 rebounds, 5.5 assists and 4.8 steals while shooting 59.4% from the field. Hidalgo is a huge threat on offense and defense and could really add to the young core already there if she goes to the Mystics. Washington could use more 3-point shooting. While Hidalgo wasn't great from beyond the arc last season (36 of 142, 25.4%), she shot 40% from 3-point range as a sophomore and is at 40% so far this season.

4. Seattle Storm: Tessa Johnson
South Carolina | guard | 6-foot-1 | senior

Johnson's 3-point shooting is an impressive tool that will translate to the pro game. She was the top power-conference player in the country last season in 3-point percentage (44.8%, 90 of 201). So far this season, she is 9-for-18 (50%) from beyond the arc and is averaging 17.0 points. She had 28 points in Sunday's victory over USC. The Storm were last in the WNBA this past season at 8-36 and could benefit from another dynamic young guard to go along with the young post talent they have.

5. Portland Fire: Mikaylah Williams
LSU | guard | 6-foot | senior

The Tigers have cruised through four blowouts, and Williams' averages -- 19.0 points, 5.3 rebounds and 5.5 assists while shooting 58% from the field and 45.5% from beyond the arc -- don't tell us anything we didn't expect. She's a pro-ready player on the offensive end who can look to improve defensively in the WNBA. The expansion Fire had a solid season in 2025, going 17-27, and Williams could fit in offensively.

6. Los Angeles Sparks: Kymora Johnson
Virginia | guard | 5-foot-7 | senior

The Cavaliers are 5-0, and we will know more about them once they play their tougher nonconference foes, such as Oklahoma on Nov. 23. But so far, Johnson has looked very good, averaging 18.8 points, 5.2 rebounds, 5.4 assists and 2.2 steals while shooting 59.6% from the field and 61.3% from beyond the arc (13 of 21). With back-to-back picks, Los Angeles can address two of several needs with this draft. The Sparks were 16-28 this season and missed the playoffs for the sixth year in a row.

7. Los Angeles Sparks: Sarah Cissé
France | forward | 6-foot-2

There's so much we don't know now about the Sparks -- including who their coach will be for 2027 -- as they move on after future Hall of Famer Nneka Ogwumike's retirement. But Cissé is another talented player out of France who could make an impact on the WNBA. The MVP of the U20 European Championships this summer, she turns 20 in January. The Sparks were next to last in the WNBA in rebounding this past season, so Cissé might be able to help there.

8. New York Liberty: Ainhoa Risacher
France | forward | 6-foot-1

If you recognize the last name, Risacher is the younger sister of Zaccharie Risacher, the NBA's No. 1 draft pick in 2024. A good-sized wing player, Risacher competed alongside Cissé on France's winning U20 European Championships team this past summer. She will turn 20 in July. The Liberty had an up-and-down 2026 season, getting the No. 8 seed in the playoffs. They knocked off No. 1 Minnesota but then were swept by No. 4 Atlanta. New York fired Chris DeMarco after just one season, so we await their next coach. The Liberty already have a strong French/international presence. The question might be if Risacher impresses them enough defensively compared with other draft options.

9. Dallas Wings: Chloe Kitts
South Carolina | forward | 6-foot-2 | senior

Kitts missed last season because of a knee injury but has looked great so far. A starter as a junior, she averaged 10.2 points and 7.7 rebounds in 2024-25. Through four games this season, she has three double-doubles and is averaging 13.0 points and 10.0 rebounds. In Sunday's victory over USC, Kitts had 15 points, 12 rebounds, three assists and four steals. If she continues to play this well, we could see her move up the draft board. Still, with Dallas having young guards such as Paige Bueckers and Azzi Fudd, Kitts could be a good addition for the Wings, who made the playoffs at 27-17 this season.

10. Indiana Fever: Talaysia Cooper
Ole Miss | guard | 6-foot-0 | senior

The Fever are facing two huge offseason questions: Will free agent guard Kelsey Mitchell return, and who will be their general manager? Indiana could use help at the wing position with a player who can defend at a high level but also score. That could be Cooper, who is playing for her third SEC program and averaging 14.0 points while shooting 37% (10 of 27) from 3-point range. She showed progress from beyond the arc last season, and if that continues this season it will help her draft prospects. Cooper had her best defensive season as a sophomore at Tennessee, and a return to that level will boost her.

11. Chicago Sky: Khamil Pierre
NC State | forward | 6-foot-2 | senior

Pierre doesn't shoot the 3 much, but she is relentless in the paint. After two strong years at Vanderbilt, she transferred to NC State and led the ACC in rebounding last season (11.9 RPG) while averaging 16.7 points and shooting 52.5% from the field. So far this season for the 4-1 Wolfpack, she is averaging 21.2 points and 8.4 rebounds while shooting 51.3%. The injury-plagued Sky went 16-28 and missed the playoffs for the third year in a row this past season. They were 13th in offensive rating and 10th in rebounding, and Pierre might help in both areas.

12. Chicago Sky: S'Mya Nichols
Kansas | guard | 6-foot | senior

Nichols is off to a little slower start than expected, averaging 12.5 points and 4.3 assists. (She averaged 17.4 and 4.6 last season.) That's why she has fallen from No. 6 in our two previous mock drafts. But to be fair, it's still early in the season. Nichols had 12 points and six assists in the Jayhawks' loss to Nebraska on Saturday. She and Kansas have another shot at a ranked team this week at Minnesota on Wednesday.

13. Dallas Wings: Kaylene Smikle
Tennessee | guard | 6-foot-0 | senior

Smikle started her career at Rutgers, then went to Maryland and is now at Tennessee. She played just seven games last year with the Terps, missing the rest of the season after knee surgery. So far this season, she is leading the 4-0 Lady Vols with 22.3 points per game, while also averaging 6.0 rebounds. She is also off to a hot start from beyond the arc at 50% (12 of 24). Smikle could add guard/wing depth for Dallas.

14. Golden State Valkyries: Oluchi Okananwa
Maryland | guard | 5-foot-10 | senior

Okananwa is averaging 14.0 points and 6.3 rebounds, but the Terps have played just three games. She was first-team All-Big Ten and all-defense last season -- we know the WNBA champion Valkyries love defense -- but she probably will need to show improvement as a 3-point shooter to ensure being a first-round pick. So far this season she is 3-for-6 from beyond the arc.

15. Minnesota Lynx: Clara Strack
Kentucky | center | 6-foot-5 | senior

Sunday was another big stats day for Strack, who had 29 points and 18 rebounds in a victory over Eastern Michigan. That included going 4-of-5 from beyond the arc, which is important: It's not easy for traditional centers to find their way in the WNBA, so having shooting range matters. Strack has shown that, making 42 3-pointers over the past two seasons. She is 8-of-21 from 3-point range so far this season. Strack, who was the SEC's defensive player of the year in 2025, is averaging 18.4 points, 9.6 rebounds and 3.8 blocks for the 5-0 Wildcats.

stories.headline: First-half romp powers Jillaroos' fourth-straight Rugby League World Cup salute
stories.summary: Australia's Jillaroos have blown away New Zealand 34-10 to win a fourth-straight Women's Rugby League World Cup.
stories.body:
Australia have underlined their women's rugby league dominance with a 34-10 annihilation of New Zealand in the World Cup final.

The Jillaroos did the damage with six first-half tries on Sunday at Suncorp Stadium, with winger Jaime Chapman recording a brilliant hat-trick before the break to cap a historic tournament.

It was Australia's fourth straight Cup triumph, following a 54-4 win in the final four years ago and coming after New Zealand won the first three tournaments between 2000-08.

Chapman carried two players more than 10 metres to score her first, before flying into the corner for another and then busting through four tacklers for a sensational 70-metre solo effort.

Her treble gave her the equal record for tries in a World Cup -- for men or women -- at 13, matching the Kiwi Ferns' Honey Hireme-Smiler from 2017.

It seemed inevitable that she would go clear in the second half.

But both teams struggled in the Brisbane humidity, with the Kiwi Ferns' try in the finals seconds the only points of an error-riddled second period.

For the Jillaroos there were several poignant narratives to come out of the win.

Coach Jess Skinner's controversial decision to play five-eighth Jesse Southwell and drop Jocelyn Kelleher paid dividends.

Southwell schemed with the ball, landed five goals and was the perfect foil for half Tarryn Aiken, who controlled play with confidence and skill.

Chapman played in the pool games and semi-final in the 2022 World Cup but has now put an indelible stamp on a final.

"There is no better win than winning the World Cup on home turf," she told Channel Seven.

"We connected the first day we came into camp."

Fullback Tamika Upton sat out the tournament four years ago with a calf injury but now the five-time premiership winner has every team accolade in the game to her credit.

Prop Millie Elliott retires with a fairytale ending while dual international Sariah Paki, who was chased by the Ferns to play for them, has now won the World Cup in two sports after triumphing with the Australian rugby sevens side in 2022.

All the talk before the clash was the danger posed by New Zealand's Golden Boot winner and strike centre Stacey Waaka.

The former rugby union star, who had scored nine tries in the tournament, was snuffed out by Jillaroos captain Isabelle Kelly, who confronted Waaka all match and gave her no space.

As the Jillaroos' big guns stood up, centre Jessica Sergis scored her 23rd try in 18 Tests with a 70m dash through the middle off an undetected forward pass.

Aiken turned second-rower Shaylee Bent inside for the second try of the match while Upton started and finished a movement that had her attacking fingerprints all over it.

Ferns fullback Apii Nicholls was her side's best player in a dynamic display until she tore a hamstring in the 66th minute.
